articles.title: Architecture styles: a field guide by differences
articles.scope: Hub that separates style, architectural pattern, design pattern and tactic. Covers Azure's six catalogued styles (N-tier, Web-Queue-Worker, Microservices, Event-driven, Big data, Big compute; page dated 2025-09-25), then styles from other guidance: modular monolith, serverless, cell-based, microkernel/plugin, broker, blackboard, SOA, and MVC/MVVM/MVU/PAC. Includes big ball of mud as the failure mode. Links messaging/microservices-vs-modular-monoliths for decomposition; the reader can pick and defend a style per bounded context.

articles.title: Layered vs N-tier architecture
articles.scope: Logical layers vs physical tiers, strict vs relaxed layering and the architecture sinkhole antipattern. Shows how layers appear in the building-block view and tiers in the deployment view (links architecture/practice for views). The reader can explain why a three-layer app can run as one tier and when tiers earn their network cost.

articles.title: Hexagonal vs clean vs onion vs vertical slice architecture
articles.scope: Ports and adapters, the inward dependency rule, how onion and clean differ in ring naming and use-case placement, and why vertical slice organises by feature instead. Notes that CPSA-F lists Onion, Hexagonal and Clean as synonyms of Ports and Adapters (R3). Includes C# and Python project layouts and test seams.

articles.title: MVC vs MVP vs MVVM vs MVU (and PAC): presentation patterns by differences
articles.scope: Who owns state, who handles input and which way data flows in MVC, MVP, MVVM, MVU and PAC (CPSA-F LG 03-08, R3). Maps Angular components with services and signals to MVVM-like binding and NgRx to MVU/Redux-style unidirectional flow, and contrasts ASP.NET Core MVC. Links frontend/angular-fundamentals and frontend/rxjs-state-management.

articles.title: Plugin (microkernel) architecture vs dependency injection vs service locator
articles.scope: Extension points, plug-in discovery, isolation and versioning compared with DI's composition root and the hidden dependencies of a service locator (CPSA-F R3). Code: Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection keyed services and collectible AssemblyLoadContext vs Python entry points and pluggy. Links architecture/practice for dependency inversion.

articles.title: Pipes and filters vs batch-sequential vs workflow orchestration
articles.scope: The CPSA-F R1 pattern: filters, pipes, push vs pull, buffering, error handling and restartability, contrasted with batch-sequential stages and centrally orchestrated workflows. Examples: Unix pipes, the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline, queue-chained functions, data pipelines and LLM prompt chains (links ai/agents). Azure Functions with queues vs Lambda with SQS, and Durable Functions vs Step Functions, in tabs.

articles.title: Stateless vs stateful services: externalising session, workflow and actor state
articles.scope: Why stateless instances scale out and fail over freely. Compares sticky sessions with distributed session state (Azure Managed Redis vs ElastiCache), durable workflow state, and virtual actors (Orleans grains, Dapr actors). Covers replication and failover of stateful services; the reader can decide where each kind of state lives.

articles.title: Event-driven architecture: topologies, event types and contracts
articles.scope: Broker vs mediator topologies, fan-out, and event notification vs event-carried state transfer vs event sourcing. Also covers ordering, eventual consistency, and event-contract governance with CloudEvents 1.0 (native in Event Grid; EventBridge uses its own envelope) and AsyncAPI, plus testing event-driven apps. Links messaging/event-driven-vs-request-response for sync vs async; Event Grid/Service Bus/Event Hubs vs EventBridge/SNS/SQS/Kinesis in tabs.

articles.title: Messages vs events vs event streams: choosing a messaging architecture
articles.scope: Command vs event vs document messages, and discrete events vs event series. Compares a queue, a topic, an event router and a partitioned log on push vs pull, ordering (sessions, FIFO message groups, partitions), retention and replay, filtering and size limits; EventBridge's newer Custom Event Bus (retention, ordered delivery, replay) is contrasted with Classic. Poison messages link messaging/delivery-semantics. Service Bus, Event Grid and Event Hubs vs SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Kinesis Data Streams and MSK in tabs; service-pair depth lives in cloud/compare.

articles.title: Serverless architecture as a style
articles.scope: Covers FaaS plus managed back ends: event sources, statelessness, cold starts, concurrency and timeout limits, the pay-per-use cost model, and antipatterns such as function-calls-function chains and recursive loops. Azure Functions and Container Apps vs Lambda and Fargate in tabs; links provider serverless-integration folders for service depth.

articles.title: Big compute and batch architectures: embarrassingly parallel vs tightly coupled, Scheduler Agent Supervisor
articles.scope: Job queues and schedulers, embarrassingly parallel vs tightly coupled workloads (InfiniBand/RDMA, placement groups), and checkpoint-restart on Spot/preemptible capacity. Also the Scheduler Agent Supervisor and Compute Resource Consolidation patterns. Azure Batch, HPC Pack and CycleCloud vs AWS Batch, ParallelCluster and Amazon EMR in tabs.

articles.title: Cell-based architecture and deployment stamps
articles.scope: Cells as full independent copies behind a thin cell router: partition-key-to-cell mapping, fixed maximum cell size, cell migration and the cell control plane. Azure's Deployment Stamps page (2026-04-28) names stamp, service unit, scale unit and cell as synonyms, so the page teaches one idea with two emphases: stamps vs geodes, deployment rings across stamps (links devops/ci-cd), and the fact that stamps are not redundant across regions by default. The provider-guidance contrast lives in cloud/compare.

articles.title: Multitenancy: tenancy models, isolation and noisy neighbours
articles.scope: Defines tenant vs deployment ('supertenants or stamps'), isolation as a spectrum, and the four Azure deployment models (automated single-tenant, fully multitenant, vertically and horizontally partitioned). Teaches the AWS SaaS Lens silo/pool/bridge vocabulary, in which silo applies to any dedicated resource. Also tenant-to-deployment mapping, per-tenant SLOs, noisy-neighbour controls and multi-tenant data access patterns; the Rosetta rows live in cloud/compare and tenant authorization in security.

articles.title: Cloud design patterns catalog with Azure and AWS mappings
articles.scope: All 44 patterns in the Azure Architecture Center catalog (dated 2026-05-03) plus the AWS Prescriptive Guidance set (API routing by hostname, path and header; retry with backoff; saga choreography and orchestration; scatter-gather; transactional outbox; hexagonal). Each entry gives the problem, pillars, trade-off, Azure and AWS implementation with fidelity, and the owning page. Federated Identity, Gatekeeper and Quarantine link to security pages; no recency claims without a dated source.

articles.title: Retry vs timeout vs circuit breaker vs bulkhead: composing a resilience pipeline
articles.scope: Transient vs persistent faults, exponential backoff with jitter, retry budgets, timeouts and deadline propagation, breaker states, bulkheads, fallback and hedging. Shows both strategy orderings and how each counts failures, using the .NET standard handler order (rate limiter, total timeout, retry, circuit breaker, attempt timeout). Code: C# Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience on Polly v8 (ConcurrencyLimiter as bulkhead, hedging, fallback) and Python tenacity + pybreaker + asyncio.timeout/Semaphore; GenAI circuit breakers and fallbacks link ai/applied.

articles.title: Throttling vs rate limiting vs queue-based load levelling vs load shedding
articles.scope: The five responses to overload: server-side throttling (including gateway 'rate limits'), caller-side pacing, buffering with queue-based load levelling plus competing consumers and priority queues, backpressure, and load shedding. Explains token and leaky bucket algorithms, plus token-per-minute model quotas. The reader can choose the response for a burst, a sustained overload or a noisy tenant.

articles.title: Caching strategies: cache-aside vs read-through vs write-through vs write-behind
articles.scope: Strategy semantics, TTL and invalidation, refresh-ahead, stampede protection, and local vs distributed vs edge caches including static content hosting behind a CDN and header-based cache keys. Contrasts exact-match caching with semantic and prompt caching (links ai/applied). .NET HybridCache and Python clients; Azure Managed Redis (Redis Enterprise based) vs ElastiCache (Valkey, Redis OSS, Memcached), Front Door vs CloudFront in tabs.

articles.title: CQRS vs event sourcing (and materialized views)
articles.scope: Why CQRS and event sourcing are independent patterns. Covers projections and read models, the Materialized View and Index Table patterns, snapshots, replay and event versioning. Links messaging/event-driven-vs-request-response for CRUD-with-events rather than repeating it.

articles.title: Saga pattern: orchestration, choreography and compensation
articles.scope: Sagas built on compensating transactions, with compensable, pivot and retriable steps, choreography vs orchestration, and saga observability. An expert section covers countermeasures for missing isolation (semantic lock, commutative updates, reread). Links messaging/outbox-pattern; Durable Functions vs Step Functions and Lambda durable functions in tabs.

articles.title: Long-running operations: async request-reply vs workflow orchestration vs durable execution
articles.scope: HTTP 202 plus a status endpoint vs callbacks and webhooks, state-machine orchestration (Step Functions, Logic Apps) vs replay-based durable execution (Durable Functions and Durable Task SDKs on Durable Task Scheduler, Lambda durable functions up to one year, Temporal). Covers determinism rules and human approval steps via Step Functions task tokens, Durable Functions external events and Lambda durable waits that suspend without compute charges, a topic also flagged in SAP-C02 Emerging Topics. Links ai/agents and ai/protocols for long-running agents.

articles.title: Strangler fig and anti-corruption layer for incremental modernization
articles.scope: Routing-based strangling, branch by abstraction, parallel run and CDC-assisted data migration, plus the ACL that keeps a legacy model out of the new one. Links architecture/migration for the 7Rs and wave planning.

articles.title: Gateway routing, offloading and aggregation vs backends for frontends
articles.scope: API gateway vs reverse proxy vs service mesh, the three gateway patterns, hostname/path/header routing, and when a BFF per client beats one shared gateway. An AI gateway section covers token-based limits, model routing and fallback, semantic caching and usage metering (product depth links ai/platforms). API Management, Application Gateway and Front Door vs API Gateway, ALB and CloudFront in tabs; links messaging/rest-vs-grpc-apis.

articles.title: Sidecar vs ambassador vs adapter: out-of-process helper patterns
articles.scope: Out-of-process helpers for cross-cutting concerns: the ambassador as an outbound proxy, the adapter container that normalises output (distinct from the GoF adapter), Dapr sidecars and sidecar-less meshes. Pod mechanics, init containers and native sidecar containers (stable since Kubernetes v1.33) link devops/kubernetes; mTLS links security/mtls-vs-api-keys.

articles.title: Valet key vs claim check: moving bulk data out of the request and message path
articles.scope: Scoped direct-access tokens (Blob SAS with stored access policies, S3 presigned URLs) vs storing large payloads and passing references through the broker. Includes dated message size limits: SQS 1 MiB and SNS 256 KiB default (configurable to 1 MiB), both with extended clients up to 2 GB via S3; Service Bus Standard 256 KB and Premium up to 100 MB over AMQP. Token hygiene links security/data-protection.

articles.title: External configuration store vs feature flags vs secrets: application configuration architecture
articles.scope: Separates configuration, secrets and feature flags. Covers the External Configuration Store pattern, dynamic refresh (sentinel keys, push notifications, C# IOptionsMonitor, Python providers), kill switches, per-environment and per-stamp configuration, safe configuration rollout with automatic rollback, and switching models or providers without redeploying. Azure App Configuration (feature management, Key Vault references, snapshots) vs AWS AppConfig with Systems Manager Parameter Store and Secrets Manager in tabs; secret handling links security.

articles.title: Enterprise integration patterns: channels, routing, transformation and endpoints
articles.scope: Point-to-point vs publish-subscribe channels, content-based router, message filter, recipient list, splitter and aggregator, scatter-gather, routing slip, process manager, message translator, content enricher, correlation identifier, canonical data model, messaging bridge and idempotent receiver. Builds on the pipes-and-filters page and maps each to Logic Apps/Service Bus/Event Grid and EventBridge/SQS/SNS/Step Functions with fidelity, including content-based routing of model requests.

articles.title: DDD strategic design and context mapping
articles.scope: Core, supporting and generic subdomains, bounded contexts, ubiquitous language and every context-map relationship: partnership, shared kernel, customer-supplier, conformist, ACL, open host service, published language, separate ways and big ball of mud. CPSA-F names DDD only as an R3 approach (LG 03-03). The reader can draw a context map and derive service boundaries.

articles.title: DDD tactical design: entities, value objects and aggregates
articles.scope: Entities vs value objects, aggregate boundaries and invariants, domain vs integration events, repositories, and domain vs application services (CPSA-F R3). Value-object mapping with C# records and EF Core complex types (EF Core 8+) vs owned types, and Python frozen dataclasses.

articles.title: How to run an event storming workshop
articles.scope: Big-picture, process-level and design-level event storming, with a worked example that ends in bounded contexts, aggregates and candidate services, plus a remote facilitation kit. Enrichment only: CPSA-F lists DDD as R3 and does not name event storming.

articles.title: Design patterns architects must recognise
articles.scope: The CPSA-F LG 03-09 set (adapter, facade, proxy, observer, strategy, template method, visitor, interpreter, combinator; R3) taught as difference tables. Covers adapter vs facade vs proxy vs decorator, strategy vs template method, and observer vs publish-subscribe vs RxJS Observable. Short C# and Python examples.

articles.title: Cloud performance and architecture antipatterns
articles.scope: Azure's antipattern catalog (busy database, busy front end, chatty I/O, extraneous fetching, improper instantiation, monolithic persistence, no caching, noisy neighbor, retry storm, synchronous I/O) plus distributed monolith, big ball of mud and recursive function chains. For each: symptoms, how to detect it in telemetry, and the pattern that fixes it.

articles.title: Fallacies of distributed computing and failure models
articles.scope: Teaches the canonical eight fallacies first, then Azure's variant (catalog dated 2026-05-03), which replaces 'transport cost is zero' and 'the network is homogeneous' with 'component versioning is simple' and 'observability implementation can be delayed'. Also covers partial failure, crash-stop/crash-recovery/omission/Byzantine faults, timing models, two generals, FLP, failure detection, gossip, and the illusion of RPC transparency (CPSA-F LG 03-12, R3).

articles.title: CAP vs PACELC: what each theorem actually says
articles.scope: A precise statement of CAP, its common misreadings, and PACELC's latency-vs-consistency branch. Classifies Cosmos DB levels, DynamoDB global tables (MREC with last-writer-wins and RPO equal to the replication delay; MRSC with exactly three Regions, RPO 0, a mode fixed at creation and Regions that may span continents), Aurora DSQL (strong consistency, Region sets only), PostgreSQL and Cassandra. The reader can classify a database for a scenario question.

articles.title: Consistency models: linearizability to eventual
articles.scope: Linearizability vs serializability vs vendor 'strong consistency', sequential and causal consistency, session guarantees, bounded staleness, consistent prefix and eventual consistency. Cosmos DB's five levels and DynamoDB per-request and global-table modes in tabs. Links data/relational-databases for isolation levels and MVCC.

articles.title: Replication: single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless (with quorums)
articles.scope: Synchronous vs asynchronous replication and its effect on RPO, replication lag and read replicas, standby vs read replicas, N/R/W quorums, read repair and anti-entropy, and conflict resolution (LWW, CRDTs, custom merge). Maps to Azure SQL geo-replication, Cosmos DB multi-region writes, Aurora Global Database and DynamoDB global tables (MREC vs MRSC).

articles.title: Consensus: Raft vs Paxos
articles.scope: The consensus problem, majority quorums, Paxos and Multi-Paxos, Raft leader election, log replication and membership changes. Shows where consensus runs (etcd in a highly available Kubernetes control plane, ZooKeeper's ZAB, KRaft as the only mode since Kafka 4.0, distributed SQL) and why consensus quorums differ from Dynamo-style quorums.

articles.title: Leader election, leases and fencing tokens
articles.scope: The Leader Election pattern, lease-based locks, split brain and fencing tokens, implemented with Azure Blob leases, DynamoDB conditional writes and Kubernetes Lease objects (used by HA controller managers and schedulers) in C# and Python.

articles.title: Partitioning and sharding: hash, range, directory and consistent hashing
articles.scope: The Sharding pattern vs in-database partitioning (links data/high-frequency-indexing-partitioning). Covers partition-key choice and cardinality, hot partitions, consistent hashing, rebalancing, cross-shard queries and search-index sharding. Cosmos DB logical/physical partitions vs DynamoDB partition keys and OpenSearch shards in tabs.

articles.title: Time, clocks and ordering
articles.scope: Clock skew, NTP/PTP and Amazon Time Sync, happens-before, Lamport and vector clocks, hybrid logical clocks and TrueTime-style bounds. Ordering guarantees in Kafka partitions, Service Bus sessions and SQS FIFO message groups (the Sequential Convoy pattern), grounding CPSA-F LG 03-12's causality goals.

articles.title: Distributed transactions: 2PC vs sagas vs outbox
articles.scope: Atomic commitment (2PC, 3PC, XA) and its blocking failure modes, try-confirm-cancel, sagas, the dual-write problem (links messaging/outbox-pattern) and distributed SQL with optimistic concurrency (Aurora DSQL). The reader can choose a consistency mechanism per business operation.

articles.title: Latency, throughput and queueing: percentiles, tail latency, Little's law and the utilisation knee
articles.scope: Percentiles vs averages, tail-latency amplification under fan-out, Little's law, and why queueing delay explodes near full utilisation. Covers turning business requirements into measurable latency and throughput objectives and finding bottlenecks with profiling and traces. This is the theory behind load shedding, hedging, autoscaling thresholds, batching, parallel model calls and metastable failures.

articles.title: Data models for architects: conceptual, logical and physical models, products vs sums, access-pattern modelling
articles.scope: Grounds CPSA-F LG 01-07 (R2): conceptual vs logical vs physical models, products vs sums, decoupling a model from its representation in databases, files and protocols, and how data shapes storage, security, scalability and reliability. Contrasts access-pattern-first modelling (DynamoDB keys, GSIs, query vs scan, single-table design; Cosmos DB embed vs reference and partition keys) with normalised relational modelling (links data/relational-databases). Serialization in C# and Python.

articles.title: OLTP vs OLAP vs HTAP
articles.scope: Workload shapes, operational vs analytical data planes, HTAP and its practical replacements (Fabric mirroring, zero-ETL integrations). Covers cost-effective database types for each workload; links data/row-vs-columnar-storage for storage layout instead of repeating it.

articles.title: Data warehouse vs data lake vs lakehouse
articles.scope: Schema-on-write vs schema-on-read, open table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg), dimensional modelling (facts, dimensions, star vs snowflake, SCDs), Kimball vs Inmon vs Data Vault, and building and securing data lakes. Fabric OneLake, Lakehouse and Warehouse (Delta-native with Iceberg metadata virtualization) plus Azure Databricks vs Redshift, S3 Tables, Lake Formation, Athena and the lakehouse architecture of Amazon SageMaker in tabs.

articles.title: Medallion architecture: bronze, silver, gold
articles.scope: Layer contracts, data-quality gates, deployment patterns (a lakehouse per layer, a warehouse for gold), Fabric materialized lake views (check release status), and how medallion maps to raw/curated/consumption zones on AWS.

articles.title: Data mesh vs data fabric vs centralized platform
articles.scope: The four data-mesh principles, data products and data contracts, federated computational governance vs metadata-driven fabric, and catalogs and lineage. Fabric domains and Microsoft Purview Unified Catalog vs SageMaker Catalog (Amazon DataZone) and Lake Formation; links security/data-protection.

articles.title: ETL vs ELT vs zero-ETL vs data virtualization
articles.scope: Where transformation runs, cost and governance implications, format conversion (CSV to Parquet), replication-based zero-ETL and Fabric mirroring, shortcuts and federated query, and reverse ETL. Data Factory and Fabric pipelines vs AWS Glue and zero-ETL integrations (targets: Redshift, SageMaker lakehouse, OpenSearch Service) in tabs.

articles.title: Change data capture: log-based, trigger-based and query-based
articles.scope: CDC mechanics, initial snapshot plus streaming, ordering and schema drift, Debezium, SQL Server CDC vs change tracking, Cosmos DB change feed vs DynamoDB Streams, and AWS DMS ongoing replication. Covers keeping vector indexes fresh via change detection; links messaging/outbox-pattern for outbox via CDC.

articles.title: Batch vs stream processing; lambda vs kappa architecture
articles.scope: Batch vs micro-batch vs streaming, event time vs processing time, tumbling/hopping/sliding/session windows, watermarks and late data, exactly-once processing (links messaging/delivery-semantics), and lambda vs kappa. Event Hubs (with Capture), Stream Analytics and Fabric Real-Time Intelligence/Eventstream vs Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose, MSK and Managed Service for Apache Flink in tabs; links messaging/redis-streams-vs-kafka.

articles.title: Polyglot persistence and choosing a data store
articles.scope: A decision procedure from access patterns to store models (relational, key-value, document, wide-column, graph, time-series, search, vector, in-memory, ledger) and the operational cost of many stores. Honest rows: ledger maps to Azure SQL Database ledger and Azure Confidential Ledger, with no AWS equivalent since Amazon QLDB reached end of support in 2025. Time series maps to Fabric Eventhouse/Azure Data Explorer vs Amazon Timestream for InfluxDB, which AWS now steers LiveAnalytics users towards.

articles.title: Vector stores as an architecture choice
articles.scope: Search index vs vector-capable operational database vs object-store vectors. Covers ANN index families (HNSW, IVF, DiskANN, quantization), filtering and tenancy, freshness and re-embedding, sharding, operations, cost and regional design. Azure AI Search, Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, Azure DocumentDB (formerly Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB vCore), Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure SQL Database and Azure Managed Redis vs Amazon OpenSearch Service/Serverless, Aurora and RDS for PostgreSQL (pgvector), Amazon S3 Vectors (best for infrequent queries; snapshots export to OpenSearch Serverless for high QPS), Amazon MemoryDB, Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) and Neptune Analytics. Only selection criteria live here; products and RAG link ai/platforms and ai/applied.

articles.title: Schema evolution: backward, forward and full compatibility
articles.scope: Compatibility modes for events and tables, schema registries (Azure Event Hubs schema registry, AWS Glue Schema Registry, EventBridge schema registry), Avro/Protobuf/JSON Schema, and Delta/Iceberg schema evolution, including what OneLake's Delta-Iceberg virtualization tolerates. API versioning links messaging/rest-vs-grpc-apis.

articles.title: High availability vs disaster recovery vs fault tolerance
articles.scope: Availability vs reliability vs resiliency vs durability; HA vs DR vs fault tolerance vs business continuity; redundancy, N+1 and single points of failure; and required availability per workload class (production vs non-production). Maps the CISSP and CCSP BC/DR vocabulary; the reader can classify any requirement into the right bucket before choosing services.

articles.title: SLA vs SLO vs SLI, composite SLAs and error budgets
articles.scope: Definitions, nines-to-downtime arithmetic, composite maths for serial and parallel dependencies (for example DynamoDB global tables at 99.999% vs 99.99% single-Region), reading provider SLA scope, MTTR/MTBF as KPIs, error budgets as a design input, and quality scenarios (CPSA-F). Links devops/sre for burn-rate alerting and error-budget policy.

articles.title: RTO, RPO and the DR strategies
articles.scope: RTO vs RPO and MTTR, and the strategies backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, hot standby (statically stable active/passive) and multi-site active/active, mapped to cold, warm and hot sites and multiple processing sites. Covers DR-Region quotas and capacity, data-plane failover (ARC routing control) vs control-plane changes, and the AWS whitepaper's advice to automate the failover steps but often initiate regional failover manually. Site Recovery (Azure-to-Azure and VMware/Hyper-V/physical to Azure) vs Elastic Disaster Recovery (any source into AWS) and ARC Region switch in tabs.

articles.title: Multi-AZ vs multi-region; active-active vs active-passive
articles.scope: Zonal vs zone-redundant vs nonzonal deployments, Region and AZ selection by latency, when multi-region is worth it, and the read-local, write-global, write-local and write-partitioned strategies. Also global routing, failover and failback, split brain, ARC routing control and readiness check (quotas, capacity, routing; not in the failover critical path), capacity reservations, and cross-AZ and cross-Region transfer cost. Front Door/Traffic Manager vs Route 53/Global Accelerator/CloudFront in tabs.

articles.title: Database high availability and DR: synchronous replicas, failover groups, global databases and read replicas
articles.scope: Engine-level HA and DR. Azure side: Azure SQL Database zone redundancy and Business Critical replicas, active geo-replication vs failover groups and listeners, PostgreSQL HA standbys and read replicas, Cosmos DB service-managed failover. AWS side: RDS Multi-AZ instance vs cluster, Aurora Global Database switchover vs failover with write forwarding, DynamoDB global tables and RDS Proxy. Covers point-in-time restore, connection handling, DNS TTL and failover testing.

articles.title: Storage redundancy and durability: local, zone, geo and read-access secondaries
articles.scope: LRS/ZRS/GRS/GZRS and read-access secondaries vs S3's multi-AZ default, single-zone S3 classes, and CRR/SRR with Replication Time Control. Covers object replication, versioning, soft delete and immutability (Object Lock, immutable blob storage) vs replication, and durability arithmetic (11 nines) vs availability SLAs. Data protection links security/data-protection.

articles.title: Backup strategy: backup vs replication vs snapshot vs archive
articles.scope: Why replication is not backup, the 3-2-1 rule, point-in-time restore, snapshots, retention and archive cost tiers, and cross-account and cross-region copies. Ransomware resilience covers immutable and logically air-gapped vaults, multiuser authorization, and cyber recovery in an isolated environment. Also restore testing. Azure Backup (Recovery Services and Backup vaults, Resiliency in Azure Cyber Recovery) vs AWS Backup (Vault Lock, logically air-gapped vaults) in tabs.

articles.title: Fault isolation: blast radius, cells, shuffle sharding and static stability
articles.scope: Fault isolation boundaries (AZ, Region, account, cell, shard), shuffle sharding, static stability, control plane vs data plane dependencies, and constant work. The reader can remediate single points of failure; links cell-based-architecture-and-deployment-stamps for implementation.

articles.title: Self-healing and automated recovery (and when not to automate failover)
articles.scope: Health probes and automatic replacement (VM scale set automatic repairs, Auto Scaling health checks, EC2 automatic recovery), load balancers routing around failed back ends, reconciliation loops (links devops/kubernetes), supervision, and auto-remediation runbooks (Azure Automation, Systems Manager Automation, AWS Config remediation). Also WAF RE:07 self-preservation, and why regional failover is often initiated by a person even when every step is automated.

articles.title: Capacity, quotas and headroom as reliability design inputs
articles.scope: N+1 and zone-loss headroom maths, capacity reservations, quota planning in standby environments, Azure's 'partition around limits' guidance, growth trends, and token and throughput quotas for model endpoints (links ai/platforms). ARC readiness check is covered as a precondition monitor. Quota mechanics link cloud/foundations.

articles.title: How to do failure mode analysis and build a health model
articles.scope: Critical-flow identification, dependency mapping, FMA worksheets (with FMEA scoring), healthy/degraded/unhealthy health models, the Health Endpoint Monitoring pattern and load-balancer health checks, and graceful degradation. Azure Monitor health models and Kubernetes probes link cloud/azure/observability and devops/kubernetes.

articles.title: Chaos engineering and resilience testing
articles.scope: Steady-state hypotheses, blast-radius control and stop conditions. Contrasts chaos experiments with load tests, game days and formal DR plan tests (read-through/tabletop, walkthrough, simulation, parallel, full interruption). Tooling tabs: Azure Chaos Studio Workspaces and Scenarios (public preview, replacing Experiments (classic): Compute Zone Down, DNS Outage, database failover, cache stampede, messaging disruption) and Availability Zone Down Drills vs AWS FIS scenarios, DynamoDB replication-pause actions and ARC autoshift practice runs. Links devops/sre and practice/tabletops for running a programme.

articles.title: Multi-region vs multi-cloud resilience: when provider diversity is worth it
articles.scope: Shared global dependencies (control planes, DNS, identity), data gravity and egress cost (links architecture/cost), portable vs native services, reversibility and exit strategy. Covers cross-cloud DR (Site Recovery for physical servers, Elastic Disaster Recovery from other clouds, Azure DocumentDB cross-cloud replication via the open-source DocumentDB engine) and regulatory concentration-risk drivers such as DORA (links security/grc). The reader can argue when a second region beats a second provider.

articles.title: What public cloud outages teach architects
articles.scope: Reads provider post-incident reviews and post-event summaries as architecture lessons: control-plane dependencies, DNS, global configuration pushes, retry storms and metastable failure. Each lesson links to the pattern that would have contained it.

articles.title: Case study: a mission-critical multi-region workload from stamps to DR drills
articles.scope: One worked scenario that combines critical flows and a health model, stamps or cells, global routing, a write-global or write-local data strategy, capacity headroom and DR drills. Implementation tabs follow Azure's mission-critical workload guidance and AWS Multi-Region Fundamentals; the guidance-vs-guidance comparison is registered in cloud/compare.

terms.definition: A named family of architectures defined by constraints on elements and their relationships, such as layered or microservices, that yields predictable quality trade-offs.
A reusable, named solution to a recurring architecture-level problem in a given context, such as Layers, Pipes and Filters or Broker.
A named, reusable solution to a recurring object- or component-level design problem, such as those catalogued by the Gang of Four.
A style that groups code into horizontal layers of responsibility where each layer depends only on the layers beneath it.
A deployment style that places logical layers on separate physical tiers, such as web, application and data servers, connected over the network.
A layered-architecture antipattern in which most requests pass through layers that add no logic, so layering adds cost without value.
A style that isolates domain logic behind ports (interfaces) so that UI, databases and other infrastructure plug in as interchangeable adapters.
A concentric-layer style with the domain model at the centre, surrounded by domain services, application services and outermost infrastructure, with all dependencies pointing inward.
A concentric-ring style in which source-code dependencies point only inward toward entities and use cases, keeping frameworks and drivers at the outer edge.
A style that organises code by feature or use case, each slice containing everything from request handling to data access, instead of by technical layer.
A style that decomposes a system into small, independently deployable services, each owning one business capability and its own data.
A single deployable application internally divided into strongly encapsulated modules with explicit interfaces, often aligned to bounded contexts.
An antipattern in which services are deployed separately but are so tightly coupled that they must change, deploy or fail together.
A system with no discernible structure, where dependencies are unmanaged and any change risks breaking unrelated parts; DDD also uses it as a context-map pattern.
A style that builds systems from coarse-grained, reusable business services with published contracts, often integrated through an enterprise service bus.
A style in which producers publish events about state changes to channels or brokers and decoupled consumers react to them asynchronously.
An event-driven style in which an event carries only a minimal signal that something changed, so consumers call back to the source for details.
An event-driven style in which events carry enough state for consumers to keep their own local copy of the data, avoiding calls back to the source.
A messaging pattern in which one published message or event is delivered to many independent consumers, typically through a topic with several subscriptions.
A style that composes managed, autoscaling, pay-per-use compute and back-end services so the team operates no servers and capacity follows demand.
The extra latency of the first request handled by a new function or container instance while the platform provisions it and initialises the runtime and code.
A style with a web front end that handles requests and a back-end worker for long-running or resource-intensive work, decoupled by a message queue.
A style for ingesting, storing, processing and analysing data too large or complex for traditional databases, combining a data lake, batch and stream processing and analytical stores.
A style that splits computationally intensive work into many tasks run across hundreds or thousands of cores, either independently or with tightly coupled communication.
A workload whose tasks run independently with no communication between them, so it scales almost linearly by adding workers.
A parallel workload whose tasks exchange data constantly while running, so it needs co-located nodes and low-latency interconnects such as InfiniBand or RDMA.
A style that runs many independent, identical copies (cells) of a workload, each serving a subset of customers through a thin router, to limit the blast radius of any failure.
The thin, highly available routing layer in a cell-based architecture that maps each request's partition key to the cell that owns it.
A pattern that splits processing into independent filters connected by pipes, so each step transforms data and passes it on and steps can be reused, reordered or scaled separately.
A data-flow style in which each processing stage runs to completion on the whole input batch before the next stage starts.
A style with a minimal core system that exposes extension points into which independently developed plug-in modules add features.
An architectural pattern in which a broker component locates servers and forwards client requests and responses, decoupling distributed components from each other's location and implementation.
An architectural pattern in which independent specialist components read and write partial solutions on a shared data store (the blackboard) under a controller until a solution emerges.
A presentation pattern that separates the model (data and rules), the view (rendering) and the controller (input handling that updates the model and selects views).
A presentation pattern in which a passive view forwards user events to a presenter that reads the model and updates the view through an interface.
A presentation pattern in which the view binds declaratively to a view model that exposes state and commands, so presentation logic can be tested without the UI.
A presentation pattern in which an immutable model is rendered by a view function and changed only by an update function that handles messages, giving unidirectional data flow.
An architectural pattern that structures an interactive system as a hierarchy of agents, each with a presentation, an abstraction (data) and a control part that mediates between them.
A technique in which an object receives the dependencies it needs from an external composer instead of constructing or looking them up itself.
A pattern in which code asks a central registry for its dependencies at run time, which hides those dependencies from the caller's signature.
A communication style in which a program invokes a procedure in another process or machine as if it were local, with arguments and results marshalled over the network.
A service whose instances keep no client or session state between requests, so any instance can serve any request and instances can be added or replaced freely.
A service whose instances hold state, such as sessions, caches or partition ownership, that must be preserved, replicated or migrated when instances fail or scale.
A load-balancer setting that routes all requests from one client to the same back-end instance, usually so in-memory session state can be reused.
A programming model, used by Orleans grains and Dapr actors, in which addressable single-threaded actors always conceptually exist and the runtime activates, places and deactivates them on demand.
An architecture in which one deployment of a system serves multiple tenants (customer organisations or groups) while keeping their data and experience isolated.
A tenant or workload that consumes a disproportionate share of shared resources and degrades performance for others on the same infrastructure.
In AWS SaaS guidance, a tenancy model in which some or all of a tenant's resources, from a database to a full stack, are dedicated to that tenant while onboarding and operations stay shared.
In AWS SaaS guidance, a tenancy model in which tenants share resources such as compute, storage and messaging.
In AWS SaaS guidance, a mixed tenancy model in which some services or layers are siloed per tenant and others are pooled.
In Azure multitenancy guidance, a mix in which some tenants (for example premium or regional ones) get dedicated deployments while others share a multitenant deployment.
In Azure multitenancy guidance, a deployment in which some components, such as the application tier, are shared by all tenants while others, such as databases, are dedicated per tenant.
A pattern that transparently repeats an operation that failed with a transient fault, usually with growing delays and a capped number of attempts.
A temporary failure, such as a dropped connection, timeout or throttling response, that is likely to succeed if retried after a short delay.
A retry delay policy that grows the wait exponentially after each failure and randomises it (for example full or decorrelated jitter) so clients do not retry in synchronised waves.
A cap on retries, expressed as a share of normal traffic or a per-request attempt limit, so retries cannot multiply load during an outage.
An antipattern in which many clients retry failed calls at once, multiplying load on a struggling dependency and delaying its recovery.
A resilience pattern that bounds how long a caller waits for an operation, failing fast so threads, connections and user time are not held indefinitely.
Passing a request's remaining time budget to every downstream call so each hop can abandon work that can no longer finish in time.
A pattern that stops calls to a failing dependency for a cooling-off period after failures cross a threshold, then lets trial calls through to test recovery.
A pattern that partitions resources such as thread pools, connections or instances into isolated pools so one failing consumer or dependency cannot exhaust capacity for others.
A latency technique that sends a duplicate request to another replica if the first has not answered within a short delay and uses whichever response arrives first.
A resilience pattern that returns an alternative result, such as a cached value, a default or a simpler model, when an operation fails or is rejected.
A pattern in which a service limits the resources a client, tenant or operation may consume and rejects or degrades excess requests to protect itself.

In Azure's catalog, a caller pacing its own requests to stay under a dependency's limits and avoid throttling errors; in API gateways the same term means server-enforced request limits (see throttling-pattern).
A rate-limiting algorithm that refills tokens at a fixed rate up to a capacity and admits a request only by taking a token, which permits short bursts.
A rate-limiting algorithm that queues requests and releases them at a constant rate, smoothing bursts and dropping arrivals when the queue is full.
Deliberately rejecting part of the incoming work, ideally the lowest-value requests, when a service nears overload so it can keep serving the rest within its latency goals.
A flow-control mechanism by which a slower consumer signals a producer to slow down or pause instead of being overwhelmed by data it cannot process.
A pattern that places a queue between producers and a service so bursts are buffered and the service processes work at its own sustainable rate.
A pattern in which multiple consumers read from one queue so each message is delivered to one consumer at a time (redelivery is possible), scaling throughput as long as handlers are idempotent.
A pattern that routes higher-priority requests through a separate or prioritised queue so they are processed before lower-priority work.
A pattern that processes related messages strictly in order within a group, such as a session or message group, while unrelated groups are processed in parallel.
A pattern that separates the model and interface used to change data (commands) from the model used to read it (queries), so each can be optimised and scaled independently.
A pattern that stores an entity's state as an append-only sequence of domain events and derives current state by replaying them.
A component that consumes an event stream and builds or updates a read model optimised for particular queries.
A pattern that precomputes and stores query-shaped views of data from one or more stores so reads avoid expensive joins or aggregations at query time.
A pattern that maintains secondary tables keyed by frequently queried fields so a store that supports only primary-key lookups can serve those queries efficiently.
A pattern that keeps data consistent across services by running a business transaction as a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action if a later step fails.
A business-level operation that semantically undoes a previously completed step, such as refunding a captured payment.
In a saga, the go/no-go step after which the saga can no longer be compensated and must run to completion through retriable steps.
In a saga, a local step that can be semantically undone by a compensating transaction if a later step fails.
In a saga, an idempotent step after the pivot that is retried until it succeeds rather than being compensated.
A saga countermeasure that flags a record as in progress at the application level, such as a PENDING status, so other transactions can detect uncommitted saga state.
Coordinating a multi-step process from a central definition, such as a state machine, that invokes each step, tracks state and handles retries, branches and errors.
A pattern in which an API accepts a long-running request immediately, returns a status location, and lets the client poll or receive a callback when processing completes.
A workflow step that suspends execution until a person approves, rejects or edits a pending action, usually by completing a callback token or raising an external event.
A pattern in which a scheduler orchestrates the steps of a distributed task, agents perform each step against remote services, and a supervisor monitors progress and triggers recovery.
A pattern that packs multiple tasks or operations into a single computational unit to raise utilisation and cut cost and management overhead.
A migration pattern that incrementally replaces a legacy system by routing one capability at a time to new components until the old system can be retired.
A technique that replaces a component in place by introducing an abstraction over it, then switching callers to a new implementation behind it while both coexist.
A migration technique that runs the legacy and new implementations side by side on the same inputs and compares their outputs before switching over.
A translating layer between two subsystems that converts one model into the other so a legacy or foreign model does not leak into the new design.
A single entry point in front of back-end services that routes requests and offloads cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, TLS termination, rate limiting and aggregation.
A pattern that exposes several back-end services or versions behind one endpoint and routes each request by host, path, header or other attributes.
A pattern that moves shared functions such as TLS termination, token validation, rate limiting and caching from each service into a gateway.
A pattern in which a gateway fans one client request out to several back-end services and combines their responses into a single reply.
A pattern that gives each client type, such as web or mobile, its own back-end service tailored to that client instead of one general-purpose API.

A pattern that deploys a helper process or container alongside an application instance, sharing its lifecycle, to add capabilities such as proxying, mTLS or telemetry without changing the application.
A specialised sidecar that acts as an out-of-process proxy for an application's outbound calls, handling retries, routing, monitoring or security on its behalf.
A multi-container pattern in which a helper container transforms an application's output, such as logs or metrics, into the format an external system expects.
A pattern that gives clients a short-lived, narrowly scoped token, such as a Blob SAS or S3 presigned URL, to read or write one storage resource directly without routing data through the application.
A pattern that stores a large message payload in external storage and sends only a reference (the claim check) through the messaging system.
A caching pattern in which the application reads from the cache first and, on a miss, loads data from the store and populates the cache itself.
A caching strategy in which the application reads only from the cache and the cache itself loads missing entries from the data store.
A caching strategy that writes each update to the cache and the data store in the same operation, so cached keys are never stale after a write.
A caching strategy that acknowledges writes once they reach the cache and persists them to the store asynchronously, risking loss of unflushed writes.
A caching strategy that reloads frequently used entries before they expire so readers rarely see a miss.
The period after which a cached entry, DNS record or stored item is treated as expired and is evicted or refreshed.
Removing or updating cached entries when the underlying data changes, explicitly or through events, so readers do not see stale data.
A surge of concurrent requests that all miss the cache for the same key, often right after it expires, and overload the back end while recomputing it.
A pattern that serves static files such as images, scripts and documents directly from object storage or a CDN instead of from application servers.
A pattern that deploys multiple independent copies of a whole solution, including its data stores, each serving a subset of tenants or a region, to scale out and isolate faults.
A pattern that deploys back-end nodes in many regions, each able to serve any user's request against globally replicated data.
A pattern that makes a message handler safe to run more than once for the same message, typically by recording processed message IDs or using naturally idempotent writes.
A pattern that moves configuration out of deployment packages into a central store that applications read, and can watch for changes, at run time.
A runtime switch that turns a code path on or off, or selects a variant, for some or all users without redeploying.
A pattern in which an application exposes endpoints that run functional checks on itself and its dependencies so load balancers and monitors can probe its health.
A pattern language of about 65 named solutions for messaging-based integration, covering channels, routing, transformation, endpoints and system management.
A messaging channel, typically a queue, that delivers each message to exactly one of its receivers.
A messaging channel, typically a topic, that delivers a copy of each published message to every interested subscriber.
An append-only, ordered and retained sequence of events, usually split into partitions, that consumers read from their own positions and can replay.
A message that asks a specific receiver to perform an action, named in the imperative, such as PlaceOrder.
A message that announces something that has already happened, named in the past tense, without expecting any particular receiver to act.
A message whose purpose is to transfer data, such as a record or file, leaving the receiver to decide what to do with it.
An event that reports a single, self-contained state change a consumer can act on immediately, such as a file being uploaded.
A continuous stream of related events, such as telemetry readings, that is meaningful mainly when analysed over time or in aggregate.
A routing component that inspects each message's content or attributes and forwards it to the channel whose rule it matches.
A routing component that discards messages not matching given criteria so a consumer receives only those it is interested in, such as a subscription filter policy.
A router that sends a copy of each message to a list of recipients computed from the message or from configuration.
An integration component that breaks a composite message into separate messages, one per element, so each can be processed independently.
An integration component that collects related messages, using a correlation identifier and a completion rule, and combines them into one message.
A pattern that broadcasts a request to several recipients in parallel and aggregates their replies into one response, usually within a timeout.
A pattern in which a message carries the ordered list of processing steps it must visit, so each step forwards it to the next.
A central component that keeps the state of a multi-step message flow and decides the next step based on intermediate results.
An integration component that converts a message from one format or data model to another so systems with different formats can communicate.
An integration component that adds missing data to a message by looking it up in an external source before passing it on.
A unique value carried by related messages, such as a request and its reply, so they can be matched and traced across services.
A shared, application-independent message format that integrating systems translate to and from, reducing pairwise translations.
A pattern that builds an intermediary which receives messages from one messaging system and forwards them to another, otherwise incompatible one.
An approach that models complex business domains collaboratively with domain experts and aligns code and boundaries with that model.
The shared, precise vocabulary that developers and domain experts use within one bounded context, in conversation and in code.
An explicit boundary within which a particular domain model and its ubiquitous language apply consistently.
A part of the business problem space, classified as core, supporting or generic according to its strategic value.
A diagram and description of bounded contexts and the integration relationships between them, such as shared kernel, customer-supplier or anti-corruption layer.
A context-map relationship in which two teams coordinate planning and integration closely because their contexts succeed or fail together.
A context-map relationship in which two bounded contexts share a small, explicitly agreed part of the model and code that neither changes without the other.
A context-map relationship in which the downstream (customer) team's needs shape the upstream (supplier) team's planning while the upstream team owns the model.
A context-map relationship in which the downstream team adopts the upstream model as is because it cannot influence the upstream team.
A context-map relationship in which an upstream context exposes a well-defined protocol or API that any downstream context can use instead of bespoke integrations.
A documented, shared exchange format, often paired with an open host service, that bounded contexts use to communicate.
A context-map decision not to integrate two bounded contexts at all because the cost of integration outweighs its benefit.
A domain object defined by a stable identity that persists while its attributes change over time.
An immutable domain object defined entirely by its attribute values, so two instances with equal values are interchangeable.
A cluster of entities and value objects treated as one consistency boundary, changed only through its root entity and saved in a single transaction.
A building block that gives the domain a collection-like interface for retrieving and storing whole aggregates while hiding persistence details.
A stateless operation that expresses domain logic which does not naturally belong to a single entity or value object.
A service that orchestrates a use case by loading aggregates, invoking domain logic and coordinating transactions, without containing business rules itself.
A record, named in the past tense in the ubiquitous language, of something significant that happened within a bounded context.
An event deliberately published across bounded-context or service boundaries as a versioned contract, usually through a broker and an outbox.
A collaborative workshop technique that maps a business process as a timeline of domain events to discover commands, aggregates and bounded contexts.
A design pattern that converts the interface of an existing class into the interface a client expects.
A design pattern that provides one simplified interface to a complex subsystem.
A design pattern that provides a surrogate with the same interface as a real object to control access to it, for example lazily, remotely or with checks.
A design pattern that wraps an object in another with the same interface to add behaviour dynamically without changing the original class.
An in-process design pattern in which a subject notifies registered observers, typically synchronously, when its state changes.
A design pattern that defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface so the algorithm can be chosen at run time.
A design pattern in which a base class fixes the skeleton of an algorithm and subclasses override specific steps.
A design pattern that separates an operation from the object structure it works on, so new operations can be added without changing the element classes.
A design pattern that represents a small language's grammar as classes and evaluates sentences by walking the resulting syntax tree.
A functional pattern that builds complex behaviour by composing small, independent functions or parsers with higher-order combining functions.
Eight false assumptions, such as 'the network is reliable' and 'latency is zero', compiled at Sun Microsystems, that lead distributed-system designers into predictable failures.
A failure in which some components of a distributed system stop or misbehave while others keep working, so the system is neither fully up nor fully down.
A failure model in which a node fails by halting and never recovers.
A failure model in which a node may halt and later restart, losing in-memory state but keeping what it wrote to durable storage.
A failure in which a component fails to send or receive some messages while otherwise behaving correctly.
A failure in which a component behaves arbitrarily, including sending conflicting or malicious messages to different parts of the system.
A network failure that splits a distributed system into groups of nodes that can communicate within a group but not with other groups.
A thought experiment showing that two parties communicating over an unreliable channel can never be certain they agree, because the last acknowledgement can always be lost.
The result by Fischer, Lynch and Paterson that no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee termination in an asynchronous system if even one process may crash.
A protocol in which nodes periodically exchange state with random peers so information such as membership or failure suspicion spreads through a cluster.
The result that during a network partition a replicated system must give up either linearizable consistency or availability for some requests.
An extension of CAP stating that with a partition a system trades availability against consistency, and otherwise trades latency against consistency.
A single-object guarantee that every operation appears to take effect atomically at one instant between its start and end, so readers see the latest completed write.

A vendor label for reads that reflect the latest acknowledged write, whose scope varies: Cosmos DB Strong is linearizable across regions, while a DynamoDB strongly consistent read on an MREC global table is current only for writes made in its own Region.
A transaction isolation guarantee that concurrent transactions produce the same result as some serial order of those transactions.
A consistency model in which all operations appear in one total order that respects each client's program order but not necessarily real-time order.
A consistency model in which all nodes see causally related writes in the same order, while concurrent unrelated writes may appear in different orders.
Client-centric guarantees, such as read-your-writes and monotonic reads, that hold within one client session even when the system as a whole is only eventually consistent.
A consistency level in which reads may lag writes, but by no more than a configured number of versions or time interval.
A consistency level in which reads may be stale but never see writes out of order, so a reader always sees some prefix of the write sequence.
A guarantee that, if no new updates are made, all replicas eventually converge to the same value, with no bound on staleness meanwhile.
The problem of getting a group of nodes, some of which may fail, to agree irrevocably on a single value or an ordered log of values.
A family of consensus protocols, including Multi-Paxos for replicated logs, in which proposers and acceptors use numbered proposals and majority quorums to agree despite crashes.
A consensus protocol designed for understandability that elects a leader by term-based voting and replicates a log to a majority of followers, as used by etcd.
The minimum number of replicas that must acknowledge a read or write for it to succeed, chosen so that read and write sets overlap.
Keeping copies of the same data on multiple nodes, zones or regions so it survives failures and can serve more reads.
A replication topology in which one node accepts all writes and streams changes to followers that serve reads and can be promoted on failure.
A replication topology in which several nodes, often in different regions, accept writes and exchange changes, requiring conflict resolution.
A replication topology in which clients write to and read from several replicas directly, using quorums, read repair and anti-entropy instead of a leader.
Replication in which a write is acknowledged only after the required replicas have durably stored it, giving zero data loss on failover at the cost of write latency.
Replication in which a write is acknowledged before replicas receive it, keeping writes fast but allowing lag and data loss up to that lag on failover.
The delay between a write committing on the primary and becoming visible on a replica, which sets replica staleness and the data loss of an asynchronous failover.
A database copy that receives changes from the primary, usually asynchronously, and serves read-only queries to offload it.
A replica kept current, often synchronously, mainly to take over as primary on failover, and which may not serve reads.
A leaderless-replication technique in which a read that finds stale replicas writes the newest value back to them.
A background process that compares replicas, often with Merkle trees, and copies missing or newer data between them so they converge.
A data structure whose concurrent updates on different replicas can always be merged deterministically, so replicas converge without coordination.
A conflict-resolution rule that keeps the concurrent update with the latest timestamp and silently discards the others.
Splitting a dataset into horizontal partitions (shards) by a key and placing them on different nodes so storage and throughput scale out.
The attribute whose value determines which partition or shard stores an item, and therefore how data and load are spread; high cardinality spreads load evenly.
Assigning items to partitions by hashing the partition key, which spreads load evenly but makes range queries span all partitions.
Assigning items to partitions by contiguous key ranges, which keeps range queries local but risks hot spots on sequential keys.
Assigning items to partitions through a lookup table that maps keys or tenants to shards, giving flexible placement at the cost of maintaining the map.
A hashing scheme that maps keys and nodes onto a ring so adding or removing a node moves only a small fraction of keys.
A partition that receives a disproportionate share of traffic because of a low-cardinality or skewed key, becoming the system's bottleneck.
A failure in which a partitioned cluster ends up with two sides that each believe they are authoritative and accept conflicting writes.
A time-limited grant of ownership or a lock that expires unless renewed, so a crashed holder cannot block others forever.
A lock coordinated across processes or machines through a database, lease service or consensus store so only one holder performs a guarded action at a time.
A monotonically increasing number issued with a lock or lease so resources can reject requests from a former holder whose lease has expired.
A coordination pattern in which instances choose one of themselves, usually through a lease or consensus, to perform work that must not run concurrently.
The partial order in which event A precedes B if they occur in that order in one process, if A sends a message that B receives, or by transitivity.
The difference between times reported by clocks on different machines at the same instant, which makes wall-clock timestamps unreliable for ordering events.
A counter attached to events and messages that yields an order consistent with causality but cannot detect concurrency.
A per-node array of counters that lets a system tell whether two events are causally ordered or concurrent.
A timestamp scheme that combines physical clock time with a logical counter so timestamps stay close to wall-clock time while respecting causality.
An atomic commitment protocol in which a coordinator asks all participants to prepare and then tells them all to commit or abort, blocking if the coordinator fails.
An atomic commitment protocol that adds a pre-commit phase to 2PC to avoid blocking on coordinator failure under synchronous assumptions, but is unsafe under network partitions.
A distributed transaction pattern in which each participant first reserves resources (try) and later confirms or cancels the reservation.
The latency of the slowest fraction of requests, such as the 99th percentile, which dominates user experience when one request fans out to many services.
The queueing relationship L = λW: the average number of items in a stable system equals their arrival rate multiplied by the average time each spends in it.
A workload of many short, concurrent reads and writes of individual records that need transactional integrity and low latency.
A workload of complex, read-heavy queries that aggregate large volumes of historical data for analysis and reporting.
An architecture that serves transactional and analytical queries on the same data with little or no copy delay.
A curated, schema-on-write analytical store that integrates data from many sources into modelled tables for reporting.
A low-cost repository, usually object storage, that keeps raw structured, semi-structured and unstructured data in native formats for later processing.
An architecture that adds warehouse capabilities such as ACID tables, schema enforcement and fast SQL to data-lake storage by using open table formats.
A lakehouse design pattern that refines data through bronze (raw), silver (cleaned and conformed) and gold (business-ready) layers.
An open specification, such as Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg or Apache Hudi, that adds a transaction log and metadata layer over data files (usually Parquet) so many engines can share ACID tables.
An open table format that records ACID transactions in a JSON transaction log with checkpoints over Parquet files; it is the native format of Microsoft Fabric and Azure Databricks.
An open table format that tracks snapshots through metadata files and manifests over data files, supports hidden partitioning and schema evolution, and underpins Amazon S3 Tables.
An approach that stores data without enforcing a schema and applies structure only when the data is queried.
An approach that validates and structures data against a defined schema when it is written, rejecting data that does not conform.
A dimensional model in which a central fact table of measurements references denormalised dimension tables that describe them.
A dimensional model in which dimension tables are normalised into multiple related tables instead of being stored denormalised.
A table in a dimensional model that stores measurements of business events, such as sales amounts, with foreign keys to dimension tables.
A table in a dimensional model that stores descriptive attributes, such as product or customer details, used to filter and group facts.
A dimension whose attribute values change over time, handled by policies such as overwriting (Type 1) or adding history rows (Type 2).
A warehouse modelling method that separates business keys (hubs), relationships (links) and descriptive history (satellites) so sources integrate incrementally and auditably.
A bottom-up data-warehouse approach that builds conformed star-schema data marts around business processes and integrates them through shared dimensions.
A top-down data-warehouse approach that first builds a normalised, integrated enterprise warehouse and then derives departmental data marts from it.
A socio-technical approach in which business domains own and publish their analytical data as products on a self-serve platform under federated governance.
A dataset published by an owning team with defined consumers, interfaces, quality guarantees and documentation, managed like a product.
A formal agreement between a data producer and its consumers that specifies schema, semantics, quality and service levels for a dataset or event stream.
An architecture that uses active metadata, catalogs and automation to integrate and govern distributed data without changing data ownership.
A searchable inventory of data assets with their metadata, ownership, classification and usage, used for discovery and governance.
The record of where data came from, how it was transformed and where it flows, used for impact analysis, debugging and compliance.
A data integration process that extracts data from sources, transforms it in a separate engine and loads the result into a target store.
A data integration process that loads raw data into the target platform first and transforms it there with the platform's own compute.

Managed, continuous replication of operational data into an analytics store, so teams build no pipelines; AWS calls these zero-ETL integrations, and Mirroring in Microsoft Fabric is the closest Azure equivalent.
Querying data where it lives through a virtual layer, such as federated queries or shortcuts, instead of copying it into a central store first.
Copying modelled data from an analytical store back into operational tools such as CRM or marketing systems so business processes can act on it.
A technique that detects and streams row-level inserts, updates and deletes from a source database, typically by reading its transaction log.
Processing a bounded, accumulated set of data in scheduled or triggered jobs, trading latency for throughput and simplicity.
A processing approach that groups incoming events into small batches handled every few seconds, giving near-real-time results with batch-style engines.
Continuous computation over unbounded event streams, using windows and watermarks to produce results with low latency.
A data-processing architecture with a batch layer for accurate recomputation and a speed layer for low-latency results, merged in a serving layer.
A data-processing architecture that handles real-time and historical processing as one stream, reprocessing by replaying the log.
The time at which an event actually occurred at its source, as recorded in the event itself.
The time at which the stream processor observes or handles an event, which can lag event time arbitrarily.
A stream processor's moving estimate that all events up to a given event time have arrived, used to close windows and decide how to treat late data.
A fixed-size, non-overlapping time window, so each event belongs to exactly one window.
A fixed-size time window that advances by a hop smaller than its size, so windows overlap and an event can belong to several.
A fixed-length window that moves with the events, producing output whenever an event enters or leaves it.
A window that groups events separated by less than a timeout gap, so its length varies with activity.
Using different data-store technologies for different parts of a system according to each part's access patterns and consistency needs.
A single database engine that supports several data models, such as document, graph and key-value, through one service.
An ANN index that clusters vectors around centroids and searches only the clusters nearest the query, cutting work at some cost in recall.
The rule, such as backward, forward or full compatibility, that decides whether data written with one schema version can be read by consumers using another.
A service that stores versioned schemas for events or messages and enforces compatibility rules when producers register new versions.
A model of the main business entities and relationships in a domain, independent of any technology.
A detailed model of entities, attributes, keys and relationships that is independent of any specific database product.
A model of how data is stored in a specific technology, including tables or documents, data types, partition keys and indexes.
A data type whose values combine several fields at once (A and B), such as a record, struct or tuple.
A data type whose values are exactly one of several alternatives (A or B), each possibly carrying its own data.
The tendency of large datasets to pull applications and services toward where the data lives, because moving data is slow, costly and risky.
The proportion of time, or of requests, in which a system can perform its required function, usually expressed in nines.
The ability of a system to perform its intended function correctly and consistently over a stated period, covering availability, correctness and recoverability.
The ability of a workload to withstand faults and recover quickly to a fully functioning state.
The probability that stored data is not lost or corrupted over time, independent of whether it can be accessed right now.
Providing duplicate components, paths or data copies so the failure of one does not stop the system.
Provisioning one more unit of capacity than peak demand needs, so the system can lose any single unit without degradation.
Designing a system with redundancy and automatic failover so it keeps serving through component or zone failures within its availability target.
The policies, tools and procedures for restoring a workload and its data after a major disruption, such as region loss or corruption, within agreed RTO and RPO.
An organisation's capability to keep critical business functions running at acceptable levels during and after a disruption, of which IT disaster recovery is one part.
The property of continuing to operate correctly, without user-visible interruption, when one or more components fail.
A contractual commitment from a provider to a customer about availability or performance, with remedies such as service credits if it is missed.
An internal, measurable reliability target for a service, such as 99.9 percent of requests succeeding over 30 days, expressed against one or more SLIs.
A quantitative measure of service behaviour, such as success rate or a latency percentile, used to judge whether an SLO is met.
The amount of unreliability an SLO permits over its window (one minus the target), which teams spend on releases and risk.
The expected availability of a flow that depends on several components, calculated by multiplying serial availabilities and combining redundant paths as parallel availability.
The maximum acceptable time between a disruption and the restoration of service.
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured as time, between the last recoverable point and the disruption.
The average time to restore service after a failure; MTTR also abbreviates mean time to repair, respond or resolve, so state which interval you measure.
The average operating time between successive failures of a repairable component or system.
The average time a non-repairable component operates before it fails.
Any component whose failure alone stops the whole system or flow from working.
Switching service from a failed or impaired primary component, zone or region to a standby, automatically or by operator decision.
Returning service from the recovery site or standby to the original primary after it has been restored and resynchronised.
A planned, coordinated role change between primary and standby, performed with replication fully caught up so no data is lost.
A redundancy topology in which every site or region serves production traffic at the same time and absorbs the load of a failed peer.
A redundancy topology in which one site serves traffic while standby sites receive replicated data and take over only on failover.
A DR configuration in which a full-capacity, already running copy of production in the recovery site receives replicated data but takes no traffic until failover, making it statically stable.
A DR strategy that runs a scaled-down but fully functional copy of production in the recovery site, which can take traffic immediately and then scale up.
A DR strategy that keeps data replicated and core infrastructure provisioned in the recovery site but leaves application capacity switched off until failover.
The lowest-cost DR strategy, which keeps backups of data, configuration and infrastructure code in another location and rebuilds the workload from them after a disaster.
A fully equipped alternate processing site with current systems and data that can take over operations within minutes to hours.
An alternate site with infrastructure and some systems ready that needs data restoration and configuration before it can take over, typically within hours to days.
An alternate site with space, power and connectivity but no ready systems or data, so recovery takes days to weeks.
A deployment whose instances or data replicas are spread across multiple availability zones in a region so it survives the loss of one zone.
A deployment pinned to one availability zone you choose, giving low intra-zone latency but no protection if that zone fails.
A deployment whose zone placement is left to the platform, so it may run in any zone and has no zone-failure guarantee; Azure calls such resources nonzonal.
Replicating data to a distant secondary region, usually asynchronously, so it survives a regional outage.
The set of users, tenants or components affected when a given failure, bad deployment or compromise occurs.
A boundary, such as a zone, region, account, cell or partition, designed so that failures inside it do not spread beyond it.
An isolation technique that assigns each customer a random small combination of workers so that two customers rarely share the same full set, limiting cross-customer impact.
The property of a system that keeps working through a dependency or zone failure without needing to change anything, such as launching capacity through a control plane.
A design in which a system does the same amount of work regardless of load or failures, for example pushing full configuration every cycle, so incidents cause no sudden work spikes.
The part of a system that creates, configures and manages resources, such as provisioning APIs, and is usually more complex and less available than the data plane.
