The part of a system that delivers its primary function in real time, such as serving requests or routing traffic, and is designed for higher availability than the control plane.
Keeping core functions available during a failure by deliberately disabling or simplifying non-essential features.
The ability of a system to detect failures and recover automatically, for example by restarting, replacing or routing around unhealthy components, without operator intervention.
A layered model of a workload's components and critical flows that maps telemetry to healthy, degraded and unhealthy states so people and automation can act on business impact.
A business-critical end-to-end path through a workload, such as checkout, that reliability design and monitoring prioritise.
A failure state in which a system stays overloaded after the original trigger is gone because a sustaining effect, such as retries or cache misses, keeps load above capacity.
The discipline of running controlled experiments that inject faults into a system to test a hypothesis about its steady-state behaviour and expose weaknesses.
The measurable statement of normal behaviour, such as an SLI staying within bounds, that a chaos experiment tries to disprove by injecting faults.
A predefined signal, such as an alarm breaching, that automatically halts a fault-injection experiment to limit harm.
A scheduled exercise in which a team simulates failures or incidents in a controlled way to practise response and validate resilience.
A planned test of a disaster recovery plan, ranging from a tabletop read-through to a full failover, that checks whether RTO and RPO can be met.
A structured review of a workload's components and dependencies to identify how each can fail, the effect of each failure and its mitigation.
A point-in-time copy of data, configuration or systems, stored separately from the source, from which you can restore after loss, corruption or deletion.
Restoring a database or store to its exact state at any chosen moment within a retention window, typically by replaying logs onto a base backup.
A point-in-time image of a volume, file share or object store, often incremental, that can be restored or copied quickly.
A protection setting that keeps deleted data recoverable for a set period before it is permanently removed.
Keeping prior versions of an object whenever it is overwritten or deleted so earlier versions can be restored.
Storage that prevents data from being modified or deleted for a retention period, even by administrators.
A backup that cannot be modified or deleted until its retention period ends, even by administrators, to protect against ransomware and insider threats.
A guideline to keep at least three copies of data on two different media or services, with one copy off-site or in another account or region.

Recovering systems and data after an attack such as ransomware by restoring verified-clean, immutable copies, often in an isolated recovery environment, rather than failing over to replicas that may also be compromised.
Spare capacity kept above expected peak so a workload can absorb spikes or the loss of an instance, zone or region without degrading.

pairs.difference: Layers are a logical code-dependency structure, while tiers are physical deployment units separated by a network; a three-layer app can run on one tier.

Hexagonal only separates the inside from adapters through ports, while clean prescribes concentric rings (entities, use cases, adapters, frameworks) with an inward dependency rule; CPSA-F lists both as synonyms of Ports and Adapters.

Both point dependencies inward, but onion names its rings after the domain model and domain/application services, while clean centres on entities and explicit use-case interactors with presenters at the edge.
A modular monolith is one deployable with enforced internal boundaries, while a distributed monolith pays the network and operational cost of services without gaining independent deployability.

SOA favours coarse, reusable enterprise services, often joined through a central ESB with shared data, while microservices favour small, independently deployable services that own their data and use dumb pipes.
EDA is about how components communicate (events through brokers), while serverless is about how compute is provisioned and billed; each can exist without the other.
A notification says only that something changed, so consumers call back for details, while event-carried state transfer ships the data so consumers keep local copies and never call back.
Any instance of a stateless service can serve any request, so scaling and failover are trivial, while a stateful service must replicate, partition or migrate state when instances change.
MVVM binds the view two-way to mutable view-model state, while MVU renders an immutable model and changes it only through messages handled by an update function, as NgRx does.
In MVC a controller handles input and picks the view, while in MVVM the view binds directly to a view model's properties and commands with no controller in between.
DI pushes dependencies in from a composition root so they appear in constructors, while a service locator lets code pull them from a registry, hiding them and making tests and reasoning harder.
In pipes and filters each step knows only its input and output and data flows through, while an orchestrator holds the process definition and state and explicitly invokes each step.
Filters stream items incrementally so stages run concurrently, while batch-sequential stages each finish the whole batch before the next begins.
Big compute is bound by CPU or GPU work over modest inputs, while big data is bound by the volume of data to store, move and scan.
Embarrassingly parallel tasks never talk to each other and suit Spot capacity, while tightly coupled tasks exchange data constantly and need co-located nodes with low-latency interconnects.

Retry assumes a fault is transient and tries again, while a breaker assumes it persists and stops calling. In the standard .NET pipeline the retry wraps the breaker, so the breaker counts individual attempts and fails fast when open, and the retry must treat that rejection as non-transient or back off past the break duration.
A circuit breaker reacts to failures by cutting calls over time, while a bulkhead pre-partitions resources so one failure cannot consume capacity reserved for others.
A retry waits for failure before trying again, while a hedge sends a parallel duplicate when a call is merely slow, trading extra load for lower tail latency.
A fallback replaces one failed operation's result, such as a cached value or a smaller model, while graceful degradation is the system-level decision to turn non-essential features off.

Throttling is enforced by the service on its callers, while Azure's Rate Limiting pattern is the caller pacing itself; API gateways use 'rate limiting' for the server-side form, so confirm which side is meant.
Throttling enforces per-client or per-tenant quotas even when the service is healthy, while load shedding drops work only when the service as a whole nears overload.
Load levelling buffers excess work to process later, accepting latency, while load shedding rejects excess work now to protect latency for what is accepted.
A token bucket allows bursts up to its capacity and then a steady rate, while a leaky bucket emits a constant rate and smooths bursts away.
With cache-aside the application loads missing entries itself, while with read-through the cache library or service loads them, so application code only talks to the cache.

Write-through persists to the store before acknowledging, so it is consistent but slower, while write-behind acknowledges from the cache and persists later, so it is faster but can lose unflushed writes.
CQRS splits read and write models, while event sourcing changes how the write model is stored; either can be used without the other.
Event sourcing records intent-level domain events as the source of truth, while CDC derives row-level changes from a database log after the fact.

2PC gives atomic commitment, and participants holding locks until the decision provide isolation, while a saga gives neither: it commits each local step at once and relies on semantic compensation, so intermediate states are visible.

Async request-reply is an API contract (202 plus a status endpoint) for one long operation, while durable execution is a runtime that persists a multi-step workflow's progress; one often fronts the other.
Orchestration services such as Step Functions or Logic Apps run a declared state-machine definition, while durable execution runs ordinary code and rebuilds its state by deterministic replay.
Strangler fig is a migration strategy that moves functionality over time, while an ACL is a translation boundary that protects a model; strangler migrations usually put an ACL at the seam.
A gateway is one shared entry point for all clients, while a BFF is a separate back end per client type, owned by that front-end team.
A sidecar is any co-deployed helper, while an ambassador is specifically a sidecar that proxies the application's outbound calls.
Valet key gives clients scoped direct access to storage, while claim check keeps large payloads off a message bus by passing a reference between services.

An external configuration store centralises settings that tune behaviour, while a feature flag is a targeted runtime switch for exposing or killing a code path; flags often live in the configuration store but have their own lifecycle and cleanup.

Azure lists 'cell' as a synonym for a stamp, so the difference is emphasis: cell-based guidance stresses a thin cell router, a fixed maximum cell size and cell migration, while stamps are framed around tenant scale units, regional placement and deployment rings.
Each stamp serves only its assigned tenants and data, while every geode node can serve any user against globally replicated data; a stamp router can itself be a geode.
A point-to-point channel (queue) gives each message to one receiver, while a publish-subscribe channel (topic) gives a copy to every subscriber.
A queue deletes a message once one consumer acknowledges it, while a stream retains ordered events so many consumer groups read at their own offsets and can replay.
A command asks one receiver to do something and can be rejected, while an event states a fact that already happened and any number of consumers may react.
A discrete event is individually actionable and suits an event router such as Event Grid or EventBridge, while an event series matters in aggregate and suits a stream such as Event Hubs or Kinesis.
Observer is an in-process, usually synchronous notification between objects, while publish-subscribe is asynchronous, broker-mediated distribution between processes.
An adapter makes one existing interface match the one a client expects, while a facade invents a new, simpler interface over a whole subsystem.
Both share the subject's interface, but a proxy controls access to the subject, while a decorator adds behaviour and can be stacked.
Domain events are internal to a bounded context and can change freely, while integration events are published contracts across contexts that must be versioned.
An entity is defined by an identity that survives attribute changes, while a value object is defined only by its values and is immutable.
CAP only describes the trade-off during a partition, while PACELC adds the everyday latency-versus-consistency trade-off when there is no partition.
Linearizability is a real-time recency guarantee on single objects, while serializability is an isolation guarantee on multi-object transactions that does not require real-time order.

Linearizability has one precise definition, while 'strong consistency' is a vendor label whose scope varies, for example a DynamoDB strongly consistent read on an MREC global table is current only for writes made in its own Region.
Eventual consistency promises only convergence, while session guarantees add read-your-writes and monotonic reads for one client, which is why Cosmos DB's Session level is the usual default.
Dynamo-style read/write quorums give overlapping replica sets but no agreed order, while consensus such as Raft uses majority quorums to agree on one ordered log.

Both need a majority to make progress, but Raft fixes a strong leader, terms and log-matching rules for understandability, while Paxos is a looser protocol family whose practical Multi-Paxos variants differ widely.
Synchronous replication gives RPO 0 but adds the replica round trip to every write, while asynchronous replication keeps writes fast but loses up to the replication lag on failover.
Single-leader avoids write conflicts but sends all writes to one place, while multi-leader allows local writes in each region at the price of conflict resolution.
Multi-leader replicates between a few write-accepting leaders, while leaderless writes go to several replicas directly and are reconciled by quorums, read repair and anti-entropy.
A read replica serves read traffic and usually lags asynchronously, while a standby exists for failover, is often synchronous and may not serve reads, as with an RDS Multi-AZ instance standby.
Sharding splits data so each node holds a different subset to scale capacity, while replication copies the same data to several nodes for availability and read scale.
Hash partitioning spreads keys evenly but scatters range queries, while range partitioning keeps ranges local but turns sequential keys such as timestamps into hot partitions.
A network partition is the fault, while split brain is the outcome when both sides keep accepting writes; quorums and fencing prevent the second without preventing the first.
A Lamport clock gives an order consistent with causality but cannot detect concurrency, while a vector clock can tell causally ordered events from concurrent ones.
OLTP runs many small transactional reads and writes on current records, while OLAP scans and aggregates large histories; data/row-vs-columnar-storage covers the storage-layout side.
A warehouse stores curated, modelled tables enforced on write, while a lake stores raw files cheaply and applies structure on read.
A lake is raw files with schema-on-read and no transactions, while a lakehouse adds ACID tables, schema enforcement and SQL performance through open table formats.
Schema-on-write rejects bad data at ingestion and makes queries simple, while schema-on-read accepts anything and pushes validation into every query.
ETL transforms before loading in a separate engine, while ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the target platform.
Data mesh decentralises ownership to domains as an organisational model, while data fabric is a technology layer that integrates data through metadata without changing ownership.
A star schema keeps each dimension in one denormalised table for simple, fast joins, while a snowflake normalises dimensions into sub-tables, saving space at the cost of more joins.

Delta Lake tracks commits in an ordered JSON log and is Fabric's native format, while Iceberg tracks snapshots through metadata trees with hidden partitioning and underpins S3 Tables; OneLake can virtualize each as the other.
Batch processes bounded data on a schedule and favours throughput, while streaming processes unbounded data continuously and favours latency, which forces it to handle event time and late data.
Lambda maintains separate batch and speed pipelines that must agree, while kappa keeps one streaming pipeline and recomputes by replaying the log.
Event time is when something happened and gives correct windows despite delays, while processing time is when the system saw it, which is simpler but shifts results whenever ingestion lags.

Polyglot persistence uses several specialised engines, each operated separately, while a multi-model database offers several models in one engine with one operational surface but fewer specialised features.

A logical model fixes entities, keys and relationships independent of any product, while a physical model commits to a store's structures, such as tables, documents, partition keys and indexes, shaped by access patterns.
HA keeps a workload running through expected component or zone failures automatically, while DR restores it after a larger disaster such as region loss or corruption, within RTO and RPO.
Business continuity keeps the business functioning, including people, processes and manual workarounds, while disaster recovery restores the IT systems and data that the business depends on.
Fault tolerance masks a failure completely with no interruption, while high availability accepts a brief failover blip and aims only to meet an availability target.
Reliability is the outcome (the system does its job correctly over time), while resiliency is the capability (withstanding faults and recovering) that produces it.

Availability is whether data or service can be reached now, while durability is whether stored data survives at all; Amazon S3 is designed for 11 nines of durability but carries a far lower availability SLA.
RTO limits how long you can be down, while RPO limits how much recent data you can lose; replication mode drives RPO and failover automation drives RTO.
RTO is a target agreed before an incident, while MTTR is the measured average of actual recoveries; MTTR consistently above RTO means the design or runbooks fall short.
An SLA is an external contract with penalties, while an SLO is an internal engineering target that is usually set stricter than the SLA.
An SLI is the measurement, such as the proportion of requests under 300 ms, while the SLO is the target value for that measurement over a window.

Backup and restore must redeploy infrastructure and restore data after the disaster, while pilot light already runs live replicated data stores and core infrastructure and only needs to switch on application capacity.
Pilot light cannot serve requests until servers are switched on and scaled, while warm standby already serves at reduced capacity and only needs to scale up.
Warm standby runs at reduced capacity and depends on control-plane scaling during failover, while hot standby already runs at full production capacity, so it is statically stable.
Both run a full-capacity copy, but hot standby takes no traffic until failover, while active-active serves users from every region and has no failover step, only traffic shifting.

Hot site is the security-exam term for an alternate facility ready to take over, while hot standby is the cloud DR strategy; both mean recovery within minutes on prebuilt capacity, but a cloud standby is deployed by infrastructure as code rather than leased.
Failover is an unplanned move after the primary fails and can lose unreplicated data, while switchover is a planned role swap after replication catches up, losing nothing.
Replication copies corruption and deletions to the replica within seconds, while point-in-time backups let you restore to before the bad change.
A zonal deployment pins to one zone you choose and fails with it, while a zone-redundant deployment spreads across zones and survives losing one.

The control plane changes configuration and is less available, while the data plane serves traffic and is built for higher availability, so failover should use only data-plane operations, such as ARC routing controls rather than editing routing weights.

Self-healing acts during a failure, by restarting, replacing or rerouting, while a statically stable system already has what it needs and does nothing, which avoids depending on control planes that may be impaired too.
A health endpoint reports one component's checks, while a health model aggregates many signals along critical flows into healthy, degraded and unhealthy states that reflect user impact.

A chaos experiment injects a bounded fault to test a steady-state hypothesis, a DR drill rehearses the recovery plan against RTO and RPO, and a load test measures behaviour under demand with no fault injected.

DR assumes the replicas are healthy and fails over to them, while cyber recovery assumes the attacker may have reached replicas and backups, so it restores verified-clean, immutable copies into an isolated environment first.

CORRECTIONS APPLIED (all checked against primary docs, 2026-10-24)
- Retry vs breaker: the .NET standard handler runs, outermost first, rate limiter, total timeout, retry, circuit breaker, attempt timeout. So the retry wraps the breaker.
- Polly v8 has no bulkhead strategy; ConcurrencyLimiter replaces it. NuGet marks Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Polly deprecated.
- Python stack: tenacity + pybreaker + asyncio.timeout/Semaphore.
- DynamoDB MRSC: exactly three Regions, either three replicas or two replicas plus a witness; Regions may be on different continents. RPO is 0. No TTL, no LSIs, no transactions. The consistency mode cannot change after creation. MREC uses last writer wins, with RPO equal to the replication delay. Global tables carry a 99.999% SLA vs 99.99% for single-Region tables.
- Aurora DSQL: PostgreSQL 16, strong consistency with snapshot isolation. Multi-Region clusters must stay within one Region set; there are no cross-continent clusters.
- Azure's Deployment Stamps page (2026-04-28) lists cell as a synonym of stamp. Stamps vs geodes is now taught here; the provider contrast moved to cloud/compare.
- Tenancy: SaaS Lens bridge is a per-service or per-layer silo/pool mix. Silo means any dedicated resource, even a per-tenant database.
- Site Recovery covers both Azure-to-Azure and VMware/Hyper-V/physical-to-Azure. Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates any source into AWS (pilot-light staging); for AWS-hosted workloads it covers EC2 only, not RDS.
- Resiliency in Azure (overview dated 2026-10-20) extends Azure Business Continuity Center. Its pillars are Infrastructure Resiliency (AZ Down Drills, Zonal Resiliency Goals and Recommendations, Recovery Orchestration Plan), Data Resiliency and Cyber Recovery. The Recovery Orchestration Plan is in preview and supports zone recovery only.
- Chaos Studio Workspaces and Scenarios are in public preview and are replacing Experiments (classic). Scenarios include Compute Zone Down and DNS Outage. Chaos Studio cites DORA as a compliance driver.
- AWS DR whitepaper: hot standby is a statically stable active/passive copy at full capacity. Use data-plane failover (ARC routing control). Automate the failover steps, but initiation is often manual. Raise DR-Region quotas in advance.
- The fallacies list is now canonical-first, then Azure's variant (the catalog page lists the replacements).
- Catalog: all 44 Azure patterns (2026-05-03) now have an owning term or article. Idempotent Consumer, Messaging Bridge and Quarantine are listed without any recency claim.
- Architecture styles: Azure lists six (page dated 2025-09-25).
- Message limits:
  - SQS: 1 MiB; the Extended Client Library goes up to 2 GB via S3.
  - SNS: 256 KiB by default, configurable to 1 MiB; extended clients go up to 2 GB.
  - Service Bus: Standard 256 KB; Premium up to 100 MB over AMQP (1 MB over HTTP).
  - EventBridge now has a Custom Event Bus with subscribers, retention up to 365 days, ordering and replay, alongside Custom Event Bus - Classic.
- S3 Vectors suits infrequent queries; for high QPS, snapshots can be exported to OpenSearch Serverless. AWS points Timestream for LiveAnalytics users to Timestream for InfluxDB.
- Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (Linux Foundation) and supports cross-cloud replication. Azure Managed Redis is based on Redis Enterprise (Redis 7.4) with active geo-replication.
- OneLake virtualizes Delta and Iceberg metadata in both directions (Iceberg V2 output, Parquet only).
- Zero-ETL targets include Amazon OpenSearch Service.
- Lambda durable functions run for up to one year, with SDKs for JS/TS, Python, Java, Go and .NET. Waits suspend without compute charges.
- Durable Task Scheduler is the recommended backend for Durable Functions and the Durable Task SDKs on any Azure compute.
